sec.title: Background and Aims
sec.p: Polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS) is a prevalent gynecological condition affecting women of reproductive age, with implications for multiple aspects of women's health. Recent research indicates that melatonin (MLT) may enhance several dimensions of this syndrome via various mechanisms. Consequently, this study was undertaken to systematically evaluate the impact of MLT supplementation on different aspects of PCOS.

sec.title: Methods
sec.p: According to the PRISMA guideline, we identified studies published between January 2013 and November 4, 2024, through a comprehensive electronic search of several reputable databases, including Web of Science (WoS), PubMed (MEDLINE), ProQuest, Scopus, and Google Scholar, utilizing MESH keywords. A meta‐analysis was conducted employing a random‐effects model, during which we computed the standardized mean differences (SMDs) along with their corresponding 95% confidence intervals.

sec.title: Results
sec.p: A total of 12 studies were incorporated into the meta‐analysis, encompassing 1590 women diagnosed with PCOS. Among these participants, 710 were assigned to the intervention group, while 692 were placed in the comparison or control group, representing data collected from six countries. The SMD for total antioxidant capacity (TAC), and endometrial thickness were 0.97 [95% CI 0.55; 1.40, p: < 0.001, τ 2: < 0.001], 0.50 [95% CI 0.29; 0.70, p: < 0.01, τ 2: 0.01, I 2: 26.38%]. Also, the risk ratio of clinical pregnancy rate after treatment was 0.38 [95% CI 0.14; 0.62, p: < 0.001, τ 2: 0.01, I 2: 13.03%], and the risk difference of clinical pregnancy rate after treatment was 0.10 [95% CI 0.05; 0.16, p: < 0.001, τ 2: < 0.001, I 2: 0%].

sec.title: Conclusion
sec.p: The administration of an appropriate dose of MLT demonstrates a notable impact on TAC, endometrial thickness, and the clinical pregnancy rate. This intervention may assist women with PCOS in effectively addressing the challenges associated with this condition, complementing standard treatment protocols.
Keywords: antioxidant, hormonal profile, infertility, insulin resistance, lipid profile, melatonin, oxidative stress, polycystic ovary syndrome

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: Polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS) is a prevalent issue among reproductive‐age women, impacting 11%–13% of this population globally [1]. The Rotterdam criteria are typically employed to diagnose PCOS and encompass these factors: oligoovulation/anovulation, signs of clinical or biochemical hyperandrogenism, and the presence of polycystic ovaries as seen in ultrasound examinations [2].

Research indicates that oxidative stress and inflammation play a significant role in the development of PCOS and contribute to the proliferation of atherosclerotic lesions in the ovaries [3]. Also, the levels of interleukin‐1β (IL‐1β), interleukin‐6 (IL‐6), and tumor necrosis factor alpha (TNF‐α) in serum and follicular fluid are elevated in women diagnosed with PCOS [4]. In this condition, heightened oxidative stress significantly contributes to the rise in the number of follicular cysts, the thickening of the follicular wall, and the absence of ovulation, especially in women with PCOS and those facing infertility [5]. Different approaches like lifestyle modifications, surgical options, and medications such as clomiphene citrate, metformin, letrozole, tamoxifen, and gonadotropins have been recommended for managing PCOS [6].

Women with PCOS have a significantly lower melatonin (MLT), a pineal hormone, level in their follicular fluid compared to healthy women, likely due to ovulatory dysfunctions in these individuals [7]. Therefore, it is hypothesized that MLT treatment could significantly preserve gonadal androgen levels and the balance of follicle‐stimulating hormones (FSH) and luteinizing hormone (LH) [8]. While preclinical studies demonstrate MLT's positive effects on ovarian function [9]. However, clinical evidence in this field remains fragmented. A 2023 review highlighted MLT's multifaceted effects but noted insufficient data on pregnancy outcomes [10], although preliminary trials report improved total antioxidant capacity (TAC) and endometrial thickness by MLT [7, 10]. Recent RCTs show conflicting results on MLT‐induced improvement of metabolic parameters in PCOS [11, 12].

On the other hand, no clear meta‐analysis has quantified MLT's effects on clinical pregnancy rates or resolved dose–response uncertainties. This study therefore aims to: (1) systematically evaluate MLT's impact on PCOS pregnancy outcomes, (2) meta‐analyze its dose‐dependent effects on oxidative/endocrine parameters, (3) review more comprehensive existing evidence, and (4) identify sources of heterogeneity across recent trials (2013–2024).

sec.title: Protocol and Registration
sec.p: Also, this systematic review was designed based on the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta‐Analyses (PRISMA) guideline [13]. This study has been registered in the International Prospective Register of Systematic Reviews (PROSPERO) under the identifier code “CRD42024536374.” The preregistered protocol (CRD42024536374) is accessible at https://www.crd.york.ac.uk/PROSPERO/view/CRD42024536374.
Also, this study was approved by “Iran University of Medical Sciences” by Ethical Code: IR.IUMS.REC.1403.246.

sec.title: Information Source and Search Strategy
sec.p: We located studies from January 2013 to November 4, 2024, by electronically searching multiple valid databases, including Web of Science (WoS), PubMed (MEDLINE), ProQuest, Scopus, and Google Scholar. In the initial phase, each keyword was searched independently, and subsequently, they were combined using “AND” or “OR” to generate new keywords or phrases (comprehensive search strategy in Supplement S1). The research librarian utilized EndNote reference management software (Version 21) for handling and automatically removing duplicate records. Also, the search strategy utilizing MeSH keywords is as follows:

“Polycystic Ovary Syndrome”[tiab] OR, “Ovary Syndrome, Polycystic”[tiab] OR, “Syndrome, Polycystic Ovary”[tiab], OR “Stein Leventhal Syndrome”[tiab] OR, “Ovarian Syndrome, Polycystic”[tiab] OR, “PCOs”[tiab] AND “Melatonin”[tiab], OR “Pineal Hormone”[tiab], OR “Pineal Gland Hormone,” OR “N‐acetyl‐5‐methoxytryptamine” AND “Supplementation”[tiab], OR “Dietary Supplement”[tiab], OR “Food Supplementation.”

sec.title: Eligibility Criteria
sec.p: Based on the PICO criteria, the guidelines for including or excluding studies for this review were as follows:
Types of participants: women with PCOS.
Types of intervention: MLT supplementation.
Type of comparison: placebo or without intervention.

Types of outcome measures: clinical and biochemical characteristics of PCOS, hormonal profile, lipid profile, ovarian reserve, insulin resistance, thyroid function, and oxidative stress. Related numerical findings of the abovementioned outcomes should be reported for inclusion.
Types of studies: all clinical trials.
Additionally, letters to the editor, comments, brief communications, conference abstracts, gray literature, review articles, and other unrelated studies were excluded.

sec.title: Selection of Evidence
sec.p: Two authors (F. A. R. and F. A.) independently gathered the data and evaluated the qualified studies, and also performed a verification check to confirm that all articles satisfied the inclusion criteria and to categorize records by study design. These authors initially reviewed the titles and abstracts of the research following the PICO criteria. When there was a disagreement between these authors, they resolved it through discussion or by bringing in a third author (Seyedeh Shahed Shoarishoar). The manuscripts that showed potentially relevant results were subsequently examined based on the outlined search strategy. All eligible studies were then reviewed in full text. If any aspects of the studies were unclear, the authors of those studies were contacted directly (Figure 1).

caption.p: The literature search results and the screening process based on the PRISMA flowchart.

sec.title: Data Extraction
sec.p: Eligible studies were reviewed separately by the two authors, who then evaluated their quality. They revisited their viewpoints afterward and addressed any disagreements that arose. The information that was extracted from the eligible studies included: region, study design, sample size, age, body mass index (BMI), intervention group, control group, duration of treatment, and evaluated parameters (Tables 1, 2, 3).

sec.title: Quality Assessment
sec.p: The risk of bias (RoB) assessment for the included studies utilized the Cochrane RoB 2 tool, following the Cochrane Handbook for Systematic Reviews of Interventions. This tool encompasses five distinct domains that are used to assess the overall bias risk [22]. This tool examines five key areas: (1) the randomization process, (2) deviations from intended interventions, (3) missing outcome data, (4) measurement of the outcome, and (5) selection of the reported results. Reviewers rated each area as “low risk,” “some concerns,” or “high risk.” Any disagreements between reviewers were addressed through discussion or by consulting a third reviewer. In Domain 2, we looked at whether the studies used intention‐to‐treat analysis or had performance bias. We categorized studies with unclear allocation concealment or baseline imbalances as having “some concerns” under Domain 1 (Table 4).

caption.p: Summary of risk of bias assessment: authors' evaluations regarding each risk of bias area for the included study.

sec.title: Data Synthesis
sec.p: A comprehensive analysis was conducted by performing a quantitative synthesis using STATA software Version 17. The random effect model was employed for the meta‐analysis due to the inclusion of studies from diverse populations. This model considers both within‐study and between‐study variances, thereby ensuring a thorough analysis [23]. All tests were set as two‐tailed at a significant level of 0.05. The Q Cochrane statistic was employed to evaluate heterogeneity, while the I 2 index was utilized to estimate the extent of heterogeneity. Heterogeneity is interpreted as (i) mild if the I 2 value is below 25%, (ii) moderate if the I 2 value ranges from 25% to 50%, (iii) severe if the I 2 value falls between 50% and 75%, and (iv) highly severe if the I 2 value exceeds 75% [24]. Standardized mean difference (SMD) was the selected key measure. The pooled SMD with its 95% confidence interval (CI) was reported. The SMD value of 0.2–0.5 is interpreted as a small effect size; 0.5–0.8 is interpreted as a moderate effect size; and > 0.8 is considered as a large effect size [25]. Due to the low number of included studies for each outcome, performing further analysis, including assessment of publication bias, small study effect, and moderation analysis, was not possible [26]. Also, the sensitivity of analysis was presented in Table 5.

sec.title: Overview of Eligible Studies
sec.p: This study examined 12 eligible studies involving 1590 women with PCOS (710 participants in the intervention group and 692 in the comparison/control group) from 6 countries (Iran = 6, Italy = 2, Spain = 1, Iraq = 1, China = 1, Bangladesh = 1). The design of the reviewed studies was as follows: nonrandomized before/after = 3, placebo‐controlled trial = 7, and no placebo = 2. Seven of the studies focused solely on women diagnosed with PCOS, while five of the studies included participants suffering from infertility in addition to PCOS. The mean age in the intervention group was 27.28 ± 2.29, and in the control/comparison group was 27.48 ± 2.37. Also, the mean BMI in the intervention group was 26.43 ± 3.01, and in the control/comparison group was 26.19 ± 2.53. In eight studies, melatonin supplementation was investigated alone, and in four studies, melatonin supplementation was investigated in addition to other supplements (magnesium, myoinositol, etc.). The minimum dose of MLT used was 1.8 mg, and the maximum amount included 100 mg. The average follow‐up period was 10.8 ± 7.55 (Table 1). The following examines the impact of melatonin on multiple factors in women diagnosed with PCOS.

sec.title: Lipid Profile
sec.p: In four studies, the effect of MLT supplementation alone [11, 12, 19] or combined [14] with other supplements on the lipid profile of PCOS women has been investigated. Among these, two studies did not show a significant effect [12, 14], and two studies showed the positive effect of MLT supplementation on LDL and cholesterol [11, 19].

The SMD for cholesterol, TG, HDL, LDL were 0.23 [95% CI −0.24; 0.70, p: 0.34, τ 2: 0.11, I 2: 60.46%, no. of observation: 3], 0.18 [95% CI −0.14; 0.50, p: 0.27, τ 2: 0.01, I 2: 18%, no. of observation: 3], 0.03 [95% CI −0.26, 0.31, p: 0.86, τ 2: < 0.001, I 2: 0%, no. of observation: 3], 0.20 [95% CI −0.09; 0.48, p: 0.18, τ 2: < 0.001, I 2: 0%, no. of observation: 3], respectively. Table 2 provides the forest plot showing the SMD of lipid profile among included studies.

sec.title: Hormonal Profile
sec.p: In eight studies, the effect of MLT alone [8, 11, 15, 17, 20] or in combination with other supplementation [14, 21] on the hormonal profile has been investigated. Five studies showed a significant effect related to testosterone [8, 12, 15, 17], three studies related to LH [15, 17, 20], two studies related to sex hormone‐binding globulin (SHBG) [14], one study related to E2 [21], one study related to FSH [11], one study related to 17OHP [11], and one study related to DHEA [14].

The SMD for LH, FSH, E2, T, and SHBG were −0.30 [95% CI −0.77; 0.16, p: 0.20, τ 2: 0.12, I 2: 69.31%, no. of observation: 3], 0.17 [95% CI −0.77; 1.10, p: 0.73, τ 2: 0.40, I 2: 89.13%, no. of observation: 2], 0.34 [95% CI −0.065; 1.33, p: 0.50, τ 2: 0.73, I 2: 95.54%, no. of observation: 2], 0.03 [95% CI −1.03; 1.09, p: 0.96, τ 2: 1.39, I 2: 95.36%, no. of observation: 5], 0.20 [95% CI −0.21; 0.61, p: 0.34, τ 2: 0.11, I 2: 63.02%, no. of observation: 4], respectively. Table 2 provides the forest plot showing the SMD of hormonal profile among the included studies.

sec.title: Ovarian Reserve
sec.p: In two studies, the effect of MLT on ovarian reserves has been stated by measuring the AMH level, one study showed a significant effect in this field [11], and one study did not show a significant relationship [15].
The SMD for AMH was −0.37 [95% CI −0.93; 0.19, p: 0.11, τ 2: 0.12, I 2: 66.94%, no. of observation: 2]. Table 2 provides the forest plot showing the SMD of ovarian reserve among included studies.

sec.title: Insulin Resistance
sec.p: Regarding insulin resistance, the effect of MLT supplementation on basal insulin and HOMA IR indices was investigated in six studies. Four studies showed a significant effect in this regard [14, 15, 17, 19] and two studies did not show a significant effect [11, 12].
The SMD for HOMA IR was −0.47 [95% CI −0.95; 0.01, p: 0.06, τ 2: 0.17, I 2: 72.21%, no. of observation: 4]. Table 2 provides the forest plot showing the SMD of HOMA IR among included studies.

sec.title: Thyroid Function
sec.p: In two studies, the effect of MLT supplementation on thyroid function (TSH and fT4 level) was investigated, and in this field, the studies did not show a significant effect [11, 14].

The SMD for TSH and fT4 were 0.09 [95% CI −1.41; 1.58, p: 0.91, τ 2: 1.11, I 2: 95.61%, no. of observation: 2], −0.09 [95% CI −0.75; 0.56, p: 0.78, τ 2: 0.18, I 2: 78.47%, no. of observation: 2], respectively. Table 2 provides the forest plot showing the SMD of thyroid function among included studies.

sec.title: Clinical Criteria
sec.p: To clinically evaluate women with PCOS and the effect of MLT supplementation on clinical indicators, the modified Freeman Gallway (mFG) score was used in three studies [8, 11, 18], and the acne and hirsutism score was used in one study [17].
The SMD for mFG score was −0.14 [95% CI −0.48; 0.19, p: 0.40, τ 2: < 0.001, I 2: 0%, no. of observation: 3]. Table 2 provides the forest plot showing the SMD of mFG score among the included studies.

sec.title: Oxidative Stress
sec.p: Two indicators have been used in two studies to evaluate the effect of MLT supplementation on oxidative stress (MDA and TAC). Both of these studies showed a significant effect for TAC in this field [8, 18], and a study for MDA also showed a significant effect [8].

The SMD for MDA and TAC were −0.17 [95% CI −0.67; 0.32, p: 0.50, τ 2: 0.04, I 2: 33.74%, no. of observation: 2], 0.97 [95% CI 0.55; 1.40, p: < 0.001, τ 2: < 0.001, I 2: 0%, no. of observation: 2], respectively. Table 2 provides the forest plot showing the SMD of oxidative stress among included studies.

sec.title: Inflammatory Indicators
sec.p: To evaluate the effect of MLT supplementation on inflammatory indices, two indices have been used in two studies (TNFα and hs‐CRP). Hs‐CRP was investigated in two studies [8, 18], and TNFα in one study [18]. Also, hs‐CRP showed a significant relationship only in one study [8].

The SMD for mFG score was 0.01 [95% CI −0.48; 0.51, p: 0.96, τ 2: 0.04, I 2: 34.17%, no. of observation: 2]. Table 2 provides the forest plot showing the SMD of the hs‐CRP score among included studies.

sec.title: Pregnancy
sec.p: The effect of MLT supplementation on endometrial thickness was stated in three studies. In two studies, a significant effect was shown [7, 15], and in one study, the effect was not significant [21].

The SMD for endometrial thickness was 0.50 [95% CI 0.29; 0.70, p: < 0.01, τ 2: 0.01, I 2: 26.38%, no. of observation: 2]. Table 2 provides the forest plot showing the SMD of the endometrial thickness among included studies.

Also, the effect of MLT supplementation on clinical pregnancy rate was evaluated in four studies. Two studies demonstrated a significant effect [7, 16], and in two studies, the effect was not significant [15, 21].

The risk ratio (RR) of clinical pregnancy rate after treatment was 0.38 [95% CI 0.14; 0.62, p: < 0.001, τ 2: 0.01, I 2: 13.03%, no. of observation: 4], and the risk difference (RD) of clinical pregnancy rate after treatment was 0.10 [95% CI 0.05; 0.16, p: < 0.001, τ 2: 0.001, I 2: 0%, no. of observation: 4]. Table 3 provides the forest plot showing the RR and RD. Table 6 shows the GRADE assessment for each outcome. The certainty of evidence varied from high for TAC to low for hormonal and lipid parameters, based on risk of bias, inconsistency, and imprecision.

caption.p: GRADE evidence profile for the main outcomes in this meta‐analysis.

sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: This systematic review and meta‐analysis reviewed data to investigate the impact of MLT supplementation on various aspects of PCOS. This study showed that MLT supplementation can have a significant effect on TAC, endometrial thickness, and clinical pregnancy.

The impact of MLT on female reproductive health involves a variety of mechanisms, such as beginning with the safeguarding of oocyte integrity and extending to its role in embryo implantation, fetal growth, and ultimately, childbirth, reducing oxidative stress, and improving uterine receptivity to successful implantation of follicles [27].

A study demonstrated that MLT exerts a protective effect against ovarian damage in rats by inhibiting the PI3K/AKT/mTOR autophagy pathway [28]. Also, the existence of MT1 and MT2 receptors within the ovarian follicle reinforces the hypothesis that MLT plays a crucial role in ovarian function [29]. Furthermore, studies have indicated that MLT can enhance the production of insulin‐like growth factor I (IGF‐I), an important growth factor in granulosa cells, that facilitates follicular maturation [30], elevated levels of MLT in preovulatory follicles contribute to the safeguarding of granulosa cells against oxidative stress, thereby playing a crucial role in mitigating the progression of PCOS through the enhancement of oocyte quality [31]. In this pathway, MLT influences GnRH via its MT1 and MT2 receptors, which leads to a reduction in GnRH receptor expression and a rise in FSH levels. Ultimately, this promotes the growth and maturation of follicles, encompassing follicle recruitment, selection, and the process of ovulation [32].

Our results showed that MLT with strong free radical scavenging activity significantly increased TAC (with a large and precise effect size (SMD = 0.97; 95% CI: 0.55–1.40; p < 0.001; I 2 = 0%)). While markers such as MDA (SMD = −0.17; 95% CI: −0.67 to 0.32; p = 0.50) and CRP (SMD = 0.01; 95% CI: −0.48 to 0.51; p = 0.96) were unaffected. MLT can reduce inflammatory responses and oxidative injury by regulating the activity of antioxidative enzymes, inhibiting the activation of nuclear factor‐kappa B, promoting glutathione production, and directly neutralizing free radicals in inflamed tissues [33]. In a similar context, a meta‐analysis revealed that MLT supplementation was associated with an increase in TAC [34]. Evidence suggested that MLT supplementation led to a reduction in systemic inflammatory markers among individuals with metabolic disorders [35]. This supports its therapeutic potential as an adjunct antioxidant therapy in PCOS, which is increasingly recognized as an oxidative stress‐related disorder. Conversely, a study indicated that a daily intake of 6 mg of MLT over 40 days did not have a significant effect on levels of hs‐CRP, TAC, and MDA in obese women [36]. Variations in study design, demographic characteristics, MLT dosage, and the length of intervention may account for the inconsistencies observed in the results of published trials.

The results of this study demonstrated that the administration of MLT significantly enhanced pregnancy rates (the pooled risk ratio (RR) was 0.38 (95% CI: 0.14–0.62; p < 0.001)), and the RD was 0.10 (95% CI: 0.05–0.16; p < 0.001), both indicating a meaningful and statistically significant increase in pregnancy rates. Notably, heterogeneity across studies was low (I 2 = 13% for RR and 0% for RD), and improved endometrial thickness (SMD = 0.50; 95% CI: 0.29–0.70; p < 0.01), with low heterogeneity (I 2 = 26.38%) in PCOS women with infertility. Similar to this study, a meta‐analysis indicated that the pregnancy rates among women undergoing ART demonstrated enhancement following the administration of MLT [37]. A systematic review encompassing 17 studies that examined the impact of MLT supplementation on ART outcomes revealed no significant influence on clinical pregnancy rates [38]. Also, MLT supplementation has been shown to markedly enhance IVF outcomes in women aged 38 years and older, resulting in a notable increase in clinical pregnancy rates (46.0% compared to 20.3%, p < 0.01) [39]. The impact of MLT on endometrial tissue and its potential therapeutic benefits in PCOS remains inadequately explored in the literature. MLT has been shown to enhance the expression of aromatase, leading to a reduction in androgen production, which subsequently contributes to a decrease in uterine volume. Additionally, MLT appears to lower the expression of IGF‐I and its receptor in cases of PCOS, suggesting a role in mitigating endometrial hyperplasia [40]. The rise in clinical pregnancy rates and improvement in endometrial thickness may indicate the combined benefits of improved oxidative status and enhanced endometrial receptivity, even without hormonal or metabolic changes. This highlights MLT's distinct role in reproductive success, separate from its effect on hormones.

However, no significant impact was observed on several other clinical and biochemical parameters (hormonal profile, lipid profile, thyroid function, ovarian reserve indicators, insulin resistance) assessed in this meta‐analysis. The GRADE assessment (Table 5) rated the certainty of evidence as low, suggesting that more high‐quality trials are needed.

No significant changes were found in key hormonal markers such as LH, FSH, estradiol, or testosterone. For instance, the effect of MLT on LH showed a modest, nonsignificant reduction (SMD = −0.30; 95% CI: −0.77 to 0.16; p = 0.20; I 2 = 69.31%), indicating moderate heterogeneity. Similarly, AMH, a marker of ovarian reserve, showed a nonsignificant reduction (SMD = −0.37; 95% CI: −0.93 to 0.19; p = 0.20). This could be due to the short duration of interventions in most studies, usually lasting 12 weeks or less [12, 15, 18], which may not be enough to produce noticeable effects on the hypothalamic, pituitary, and gonadal axis. Also, differences in baseline hormone levels, PCOS types, and variations in research methods might have led to inconsistent hormonal responses.

MLT had no significant effect on lipid parameters like TC, LDL, HDL, and triglycerides. For example, the SMD for TC was 0.23 (95% CI: −0.24 to 0.70; p = 0.34), and for triglycerides 0.18 (95% CI: −0.14 to 0.50; p = 0.27). However, the wide CIs, particularly for LDL (SMD = 0.20; 95% CI: −0.09 to 0.48), suggest a lack of precision, possibly due to small sample sizes. Furthermore, the absence of heterogeneity (I 2 = 0%) for LDL and HDL implies consistent findings across studies, yet still not clinically meaningful. This might indicate that lipid metabolism is influenced by various factors [41]. It may need longer intervention periods or changes in lifestyle to see significant changes. Additionally, none of the studies specifically focused on dyslipidemia as an outcome. Few studies adequately controlled for diet or physical activity.

Markers of ovarian reserve, especially AMH, were not significantly affected by MLT supplementation. AMH levels indicate the number of preantral and small antral follicles [42]. Since MLT mainly acts as an antioxidant rather than promoting follicle development, it is not surprising that there was no effect on AMH. Additionally, differences in ovarian reserve status at the start of the studies might have mixed up the results.

The meta‐analysis did not find significant improvements in HOMA‐IR or fasting insulin levels (SMD = −0.47; 95% CI: −0.95 to 0.01; p = 0.06). Although researchers have suggested that MLT may improve insulin sensitivity through circadian regulation and antioxidant effects [43]. The moderate heterogeneity (I 2 = 72.21%) and relatively narrow CI suggest that the observed effect might become significant with additional high‐quality trials. However, some participants were also taking insulin‐sensitizing agents like metformin, and various MLT dosage intakes, which may have complicated the effects of MLT.

No significant changes were observed in thyroid hormones (TSH, T3, T4). For example, TSH had an SMD of 0.09 (95% CI: −1.41 to 1.58; p = 0.91), and T4 had an SMD of −0.09 (95% CI: −0.75 to 0.56; p = 0.78), both with high heterogeneity (I 2 > 78%). This suggests that MLT supplementation at the specified doses and durations might not greatly affect the hypothalamic–pituitary–thyroid axis in women with PCOS. This could be partly because most participants had normal thyroid function at the start, which limited the opportunity for noticeable improvement.

To address concerns about including nonrandomized studies, we performed a sensitivity analysis that only included randomized controlled trials (RCTs). The results were mostly consistent across most outcomes (Table 5), which shows the findings are reliable. Notably, the effect of melatonin on TAC, endometrial thickness, and clinical pregnancy remained significant when limited to RCTs. This suggests that the conclusions are not influenced by low‐quality designs.

A notable strength of the current research lies in the extensive array of studies incorporated into the analysis, encompassing a diverse range of research from various countries, which may facilitate more informed decision‐making regarding the findings. Nevertheless, the limited number of studies and the small sample sizes, high heterogeneity in some outcomes (I 2 up to 95%), and variation in administering MLT dosage across studies (1.8–100 mg/day) and duration of therapy present challenges to generalizability. Consequently, future investigations in this area should employ larger sample sizes, standardized dosages of melatonin, longer follow‐up durations, and subgroup analyses based on PCOS phenotypes or metabolic status to enhance the robustness of the conclusions drawn.

Although significant efforts were made to perform a thorough and precise search across various scientific databases, there is a possibility that some pertinent studies were overlooked. This may be attributed to constraints in resource accessibility, the selection of particular search terms, or the restricted publication of certain articles. Furthermore, while the quality of the studies was evaluated using established and validated assessment tools, the potential for human error in scoring or interpreting the evaluation criteria cannot be entirely ruled out. These limitations may affect the outcomes, even though considerable measures were taken to reduce such biases.

sec.title: Conclusion
sec.p: This meta‐analysis shows that MLT supplementation (3–10 mg/day) significantly increases TAC (SMD 0.97, p < 0.001) and endometrial thickness (SMD 0.50, p < 0.01) in women with PCOS. This suggests that melatonin may help with oxidative stress and fertility. Preliminary evidence points to possible benefits for clinical pregnancy rates (RR 0.38, p < 0.001), but these results need to be confirmed in larger studies. No significant effects were found for hormonal profiles (LH p = 0.20; FSH p = 0.73; testosterone p = 0.96), metabolic parameters (HOMA‐IR p = 0.06), or lipid profiles (all p > 0.05). This approach offers a cost‐effective and accessible supplement for women with PCOS to enhance their treatment experience and ultimately attain improved health outcomes. However, because of high variability (I 2 up to 95%) and small sample sizes, future standardized RCTs should determine the best dosing and categorize patients by PCOS types before clinical use.
